en: The Terminology of Sāṃkhya.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Homage to the venerable teachers, the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrtis.
We shall explain our own experience according to our understanding:
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, to Prakṛti, and to Puruṣa;
to the secret essence of the Vedānta, whose nature is the reality of Sāṅkhya. (1)
The vision of the reality of the knowledge of truth should not be given to other yogins who are paramahaṃsas, for the world is deluded by illusion.
And when some fortunate person, for the sake of attaining nirvāṇa, speaks through a pretext that brings about his rest, he is called a listener to the sound.
He who perceives mere grammatical inflection is far from true knowledge.
Now, regarding the teacher:
through the skillful means and grace of the teacher, one gains insight into the core of the treatise. (4)
The Guru is said to be of two kinds: the Vārttika and the Āmnāya.
The Vārttika is through the state of devotion, while the Āmnāya is the Root Karikā.
But those who worship the faces of the Brāhmaṇa, the woman, and the Śūdra are the Vārttikas;
that which is proclaimed as the Āmnāya is transmitted through the lineage of renunciation and so forth. // 6 //
In the beginning were Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Vasiṣṭha;
then Śakti, Pārāśara, Vyāsa, Śuka, and likewise Gauḍa.
From those worthy of worship at the feet of Govinda, Śaṅkara, the supreme benefactor, received it;
this lineage has been declared, which bestows the accomplishment of the Guru’s tradition.
The teacher who imparts the Gāyatrī, the teacher who nourishes one's body,
and the true teacher (sadguru) who bestows liberation— this is the threefold definition of a teacher.
The study of mantras, their exposition, the ritual systems, the servants, Vedic knowledge, and the science of crafts—these are said to belong to that illustrious Guru. (9)
Having abandoned the relationship of cause and effect, he is the one who brings about perfect awakening;
he is the savior and the giver of liberation, and is called the True Guru. // 10 //
Now, regarding the disciple:
the guru should uplift that disciple who possesses a mind free from desire, endowed with faith and devotion to the guru, and who seeks liberation rather than worldly hope. (11)
O Lord, O ocean of compassion, I now entreat you:
O treasure-house of mercy, grant liberation from the scorching forest fire of saṃsāra! (12)
In this [treatise], the meaning of the Vedas—which was previously only superficially understood through the study of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences according to rule—is [now] revealed.
And thus says the Śruti: "With fuel in hand, one should approach a preceptor who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) and established in Brahman, and follow him."
For that [is attained] indeed through prostration, thorough inquiry, and service.
The wise, who perceive reality as it truly is, will impart that knowledge to you.
"Knowing which, there is no more delusion"—thus it is said in the Gītā.
O dear one, if you desire enjoyment, abandon sense-objects as if they were poison.
One who is greedy for the company of the virtuous experiences ultimate happiness. // 14 //
Thus ends the lineage of gurus.
Now, he explains knowledge according to the Sāṃkhya tradition.
In that regard, first, for one who is endowed with the fourfold means [of qualification], there is detachment from the enjoyment of the fruits of objects here and hereafter.
The second is the hexad beginning with tranquility and self-control;
the third is the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities;
the fourth is the desire for liberation, that is, the longing for mokṣa.
But here, indeed, is detachment from the enjoyment of objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women;
there, indeed, is the lack of desire for the enjoyments of heaven and so forth;
and tranquility (śama) is the restraint of the mind.
Self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the senses;
forbearance (*titikṣā*) is the endurance of extremes such as cold and heat, as well as the superiority of others;
and composure (*samādhāna*) is that which is distinct from the illusory nature of creation and so forth.
Faith is devotion toward the guru and the spiritual scriptures; cessation is that which transcends cause and effect;
the Self is eternal.
All visible objects are impermanent;
therefore, one should thereafter desire liberation.
Thus ends the fourfold means.
Kambala, Kharparī, and Veṇu are the three characteristics of the Buddha;
they correspond to the three stages of the mind: distraction, movement, and absorption. // 1 //
Now, regarding the preliminary stages (*bhūmikā*):
distraction consists of delighting in sense objects;
it is characterized by coming and going, and its nature is doubt.

The fourth state is absorption (*sulīnatā*), which takes the form of bliss. Now, regarding the intellects: although the teacher awakens [the disciple] through the reasoning of the scriptures and so forth, [the mind] remains empty, like a lump of wool.
It does not become an excessive light, like the aperture of a skull-cup;
rather, it expands through various methods, like a split bamboo cane or like oil upon water.
In that regard, first comes dispassion (*vairāgya*).

In this regard, the authoritative scripture (*śruti*) states: "Indeed, O dear one, it is not for the sake of desire for all things that all things become dear; rather, it is for the sake of desire for the Self (*ātman*) that all things become dear.
And in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "By renunciation alone they have attained immortality.
In that context, first there is the renunciation of the variegated (*śabala*).
Excrement and urine are foul-smelling, a dwelling for worms, and impermanent;
yet fools, conceited with the notions of "I" and "mine," consider that to be happiness. (1)
To whom do mother and father belong? To whom do brother and uterine sibling belong?
To whom does wife and son belong? For men, they are but bonds of karma. // 2 //
One should view wife, children, home, fields, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth with equanimity as one who is indifferent, seeing all such things as being as useless as they are within oneself.
Having abandoned from afar the company of women and those who associate with women, the self-possessed man,
patient and dwelling in solitude, should meditate upon Me without sloth.
Having entered the forest of the body, the mighty tiger among men devours all the worlds—gods, serpents, and humans alike. (5)
Having made firm the sword of knowledge and using detachment as the purification of the ground—for whom is battle difficult to win? Who is that hero who possesses self-mastery? (6)
Now, regarding pure renunciation:
Having mastered the scriptures, the wise person, intent upon knowledge and realization, should discard the scripture entirely, just as one seeking grain discards the straw. (7)
If you desire the state of Brahman, then listen to it from the perspective of realized knowledge:
detachment from all objects and the sense of self-identity toward all beings. (8)
If you desire liberation, then abandon the objects of the senses like poison;
cultivate forgiveness, integrity, compassion, contentment, and truth as if they were nectar.
The yogi meditates with the mind, just as a miser longs for wealth;
and by drinking through that mind, he has conquered the three worlds.
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing,
devoid of the sense of "mine," and free from egoism, attains peace.
Possessing nothing, self-controlled, tranquil, and even-minded,
he should abandon the marks and stages of life and wander beyond the scope of prescribed rules.
And listen, O dear one, to that [nature] within the body, characterized by both the hidden and the manifest;
it possesses ten hidden aspects, liberation as the twelfth, and is the state of the innate (sahaja). (13)
I shall constantly follow the sage who is free from dependence, peaceful, without enmity, and possessed of equal vision, and purify myself with the dust of his feet.
O Śambhu, when shall I become capable of uprooting karma—solitary, free from desire, peaceful, using my hands as a bowl, and clothed only by the directions? (15)
Renouncing all dharmas, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins, do not grieve. 16.
Having attained the state of non-objectification and the mind having dissolved therein, all activities cease; that yogi is supreme and beyond the qualities (nirguṇa). // 17 //
The delusion of the mind, which draws upon the objects of the senses as its cause, rolls about toward a single husband, just as many co-wives roll about their one husband. (18)
Excellent, excellent! Listen to your own true interest: stay far away from this machine of bones;
for in this world, the sense of "mine" regarding its parts is like that of a dog. (19)
Listen, my dear: two things must be abandoned—hope and likewise dissension.
Through hope one brings about wretchedness, and dissension increases further division. (20)
"By means of weeping and laughing, one should take recourse in the state of a *piśāca*; always abandoning attachment to this [world], remain forever as pure consciousness alone. (21)
Just as the effect of a shadow does not truly exist, so indeed is this body; abandoning the essence of worldly attachment, take refuge in the supreme state. // 22 //

O Rāma, for one adorned with dispassion, a cow’s footprint is the earth, Mount Meru is a mere post, and the three worlds are a trifle like a small seal-ring; among thousands of men, only someone rare strives for perfection.
Thus ends the section on detachment.
Now, through the door of devotion, there is fourfold liberation:
one attains union with the syllables of the Veda, similarity of form, and residence in the same world.
First is the purification of the mind and the two types of mental worship;
third is constant meditation, and the fourth is the all-pervasive [yoga]. // 1 //
The fifth, however, is the supportless state, the ground of liberation, in due order;
a mortal should accomplish it with effort, and for him there is liberation without a doubt. // 2 //
Through the means of recitation and practice, purification of the mind is ordained;
thereafter, the fourfold liberation [is attained]. Listen well, O best of the twice-born! (3)
Through mental [devotion], there is attainment of the world [of the deity], as well as constant proximity to him;
likewise, his eternal true nature is attained through the supportless [samādhi].
Whosoever worship whichever deities, they all go to the fourfold liberation;
yet without self-knowledge regarding the Being-Consciousness-Bliss Self (saccidātman), liberation cannot occur. // 5 //
However—
one should meditate upon the mental form, which is a corporeal image seated upon a throne;
steady like a lamp in a windless place, one should worship it with the sixteen types of offerings according to one's understanding.
Whether he is moving or standing still, there is no appearance of proximity for him;
he alone perceives his own true nature abiding in all beings.
Thereafter, that state of union shines forth as if it were open space.
Thus, worship of these four kinds is liberation.
Now, regarding non-dual devotion:
devotion consists in the realization that everything is composed of the Lord, and knowledge is the vision of non-duality.
Detachment is independent, and the mind is liberated and devoid of objects. // 1 //
However, one should contemplate the form of the Lord within all beings, from the outcaste (cāṇḍāla) up to the Brahmin;
one should worship them with the sixteen services as is appropriate.
That is devotion, not [the worship of] an image.

Having realized the non-difference of all beings from Brahmā down to a tiny ant, as if they were one's own body, and having unified that knowledge with the bodies of others and the limbs of one's own body, one should perceive a single mass everywhere. From Brahmā down to the stationary objects, being free from desire for this world or the next—this is what is called liberation (*mukti*); it is a state devoid of mental activity (*vṛtti*).
In this regard, the authoritative proof is as follows:
"He who perceives the nature of the Blessed Lord within all beings, and perceives all beings within his own self—he is the most excellent Bhāgavata. (2)
When one perceives the distinctness of beings as abiding in the One, and likewise their expansion from that very source, then one attains Brahman. // 3 //
When one abandons all desires residing in the mind, O Pārtha,
and is satisfied with the Self alone through the Self, that person, even while sleeping, does not suffer.
In the Gītās:
"That dispassion which indeed arises toward all things from Brahmā down to the level of stationary objects, being just like the dispassion one feels toward crow-dung, is truly stainless. (5)
Thus concludes the section on non-dual devotion. Now follows the determination of discriminative knowledge:
freedom from anger, dispassion, mastery over the senses, forbearance, compassion, tranquility, and being beloved by people.
Giving without greed is the cause for liberation from existence; these ten characteristics are the marks of knowledge. // 1 //
Karma, the inner reality, the knowledge of Brahman which is beyond that, and Indra as the fourfold meaning of the word—this is the definition of the Self, bringing about happiness. (2)

The living being becomes a knower of action, a person known as the inner self (adhyātma), a lord, and a knower of reality; and the realization that "all is Brahman" constitutes the state of Brahmanhood.
Devoted to the duties of the castes and stages of life, and to rites such as the *hotṛ* priestly functions,
they practice toward all beings that which is known as the "knowledge of action" (*karma-jñāna*).
For him from whom illusion has departed, there is detachment and the inner science;
there is inquiry, reflection, and superimposition, as well as that knowledge designated as "inner science."
Having observed the ritual procedures for the performance of dharma and action according to the systems of Dharma, Sāṃkhya, and so forth,
that which is called the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is said to be distinct from their objects.
When the meaning of the words and sentences regarding samādhi functions as the form of Brahman—being solitary, free from desire, and tranquil—that is then called the knowledge of Brahman. (7)
In that [state] where words cease and all mental signs have dissolved,
one shines by oneself, established in one's own true nature, like oneself to oneself.

The soul that possesses its own intellect for everything while being devoid of the prescribed conduct, and pursues its own self-interest regarding objects such as wealth and the like, is designated as "low. (9)
A man who is constantly devoted to right conduct, who has transcended dualities, who is free from desire, and who subsists on dry food alone—he is called such. (10)

One who is free from desire and anger, possessing only as much clothing as a staff or a rag, and whose contentment has been tasted by the female bees [of the senses], is called a Lord (Īśvara). // 11 //
Clad in the directions, experiencing bliss that is self-known and devoid of self or other,
he who eats from the palm of his hand shines as Brahmā over the earth.
That which has been performed throughout one's entire life, free from the constraints of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama),
and which constitutes right conduct— that person who delights in the Self shines forth. Thus [ends the section] on the Dharmaśāstra.
The fruit of action is threefold: undesirable, desirable, and mixed.

Likewise, the "mixed with cattle" (paśumiśra) and the "knower" (jñānin), along with the fivefold object of knowledge (siddhajñeya)—that which is endowed with these characteristics is described according to the distinctions of their modes of being (vṛttibheda). // 14 //
Having spoken again and again for the sake of some business, one should then acquire wealth;
those who are devoted to their genitals and bellies for their own self-interest—this is remembered as the characteristic of a true beast.
Those who proceed according to the conduct of the age (yuga) and follow the recognized system of castes and stages of life,
yet do not know their own true purpose— that is remembered as the "mixed" characteristic.

One who knows the entire meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures, who follows the prescribed conduct and is devoted to it, and who speaks words only after having reflected as prescribed—he is characterized as a man of knowledge. // 17 //
The wise one should accomplish that which he has said, even if the task must be performed otherwise; he should speak of goals already gathered—this is called the characteristic of success.

Having abandoned the state of being an agent of cause and effect, one should wander the earth; free from desire even for praise, one should abide in bliss characterized by the object of knowledge. 19.
Thus concludes the determination of the knowledge of world-weariness.
Dharmas based on the body, caste, and social order are constructed by the imagination;
they must be cast off like a snake’s skin, for I am that one who is stainless. (20)
From that knowledge comes liberation, according to such scriptural texts as "By knowledge alone [is attained]"; and the *Gītā* states, "Actions are burnt by the fire of knowledge.
Knowledge derived from the scriptures is indirect (*parokṣa*), while the eternal is direct (*aparokṣa*).
The first consists of birth and actions; the second is of the nature of Being-Consciousness (*saccidātman*). (21)
It is joined with the elements as their origin, sustenance, and dissolution;
and therein the Self is both the witness and the observer of the world, like the sun. // 22 //
One should view the world as having the form of the manifestation of the elements and so forth, both the immobile and the mobile; indeed, it is like a magical illusion and like a wave.
Bound by conceptual construction, the person always speaks with faults; his body dances in the street until he falls to the ground. (24)
Why do people speak various words regarding the state of being a fool or a demon, as if they were possessed by a host of spirits? For what purpose [do they speak] concerning pleasure and pain? (25)
There exists that which is named existence, luminosity, loveliness, stability, and instability;
these four forms of desire must be abandoned. I am this one alone, stainless. 26.
And she exists as the path of the Mātṛkā through the universal illusion; know that within her is that Sound (nāda), by which the objectless is perceived as an object. (27)
But the body is always devoid of mind, just as a village is without people;
even Brahmā and others cannot be its creator, for it is a mere beast and a destroyer of the self. (28)
The highest [form of devotion] is absorption in *laya*; meditation and *dhāraṇā* are middling; worship of images is inferior; and singing and dancing are the lowest of the low. (29)
Bathing is the abandonment of mental impurity; purity is the restraint of the senses;
knowledge is the vision of non-duality; and meditation is the mind free from objects.
Like a barren woman’s son, a visible sign is useless;
the eternal Brahman is itself the Self, whose singular form is the mind. // 31 //

As long as there is the conceit of "I am the body," so many actions— though they may be full of the meaning of Śruti and Smṛti and possess the fragrance of the mind through meditative absorption— are fruitless.
Attached to the karma of saṃsāra, he thinks "I am Brahman";
one who has fallen away from both karma and Brahman should be abandoned like an outcaste.
For one whose distraction from samādhi consists of various types of reasoning,
there are not so many causes of delusion until the dissolution of the body.
One is a forest-dweller and a practitioner of yoga; likewise, the second is a village-dweller; and the third is a city-dweller—this, I consider, is the way for those who dwell in the forest. (35)
The Vedas, Shastras, Puranas, and various elegant arguments [are employed];
yet the intellect is characterized by resolute determination, not by the form of mere means.
Having constantly churned the four Vedas and all the scriptures,
he who indeed does not know the essential truth is like one who tastes only the surface of food cooked on a ladle.
If one who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman) should bathe in the Supreme [Brahman],
his labor is indeed fruitless, like that of a guardian of a cow that does not yield milk.
In that mirror of space wherein the entire world appears,
all that is of the nature of Brahman and is a manifestation of Māyā.
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man keeps watch;
that wherein all beings keep watch is night for the sage who sees.
I am not the body, nor the vital breaths, nor likewise the sense organs; I am not the mind, alas, nor the intellect, nor indeed the heart-mind (citta), nor the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
I am not a human, nor a god, nor a yakṣa; I am not a brahmin, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra.
I am not a student of sacred knowledge, nor a householder, nor a forest-dweller, nor a mendicant; rather, I am the very form of innate awakening.
The activity of cause and effect is of three kinds, constructed by conceptualization;
joined with mind and ego, it is useless and merely a string of words.
Free from desire, the yogi utters sound within sound for the sake of knowledge, just as resonance exists within musical instruments through dependence upon them. // 44 //
The yogi performs all activities within the functions of the body;
even childhood play and everything else is entirely based on false causes.
Whatever a person performs, that man shines in his own home;
whatever disposition each individual possesses, according to that, such is their happiness.
All such striving for sensual desires becomes futile in the long run;
for him, no action whatsoever exists here, nor does it ever have any effect at any time.
One should understand that true knowledge is indeed that knowledge which realizes: "I am the mover; it is [the body] that moves in all actions," through constant mindfulness. 48.
By whomsoever a lake is filled, his power to give shines forth;
yet even with a small leak, one should first perform the water-rites for oneself with the mind.
Having abandoned bondage, let them act with full composure and a tranquil mind; for he who always practices this method is indeed the most excellent among the wise. (50)
All actions, beginning with the body, are known within both knowledge and ignorance;
know that "I am He" by way of the nature of pure consciousness, which is the defining characteristic of Brahman. 51.
"I am the fool; I am the knower; that which is taught as Dharma—I am that.
Know me to have the characteristic of Brahman, in the form of pure consciousness alone. (52)
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (53)
Brahman is distinct from the world, and there is nothing other than Brahman;
within Brahman, the consciousness that appears as the world shines falsely, like a mirage in the desert.

For the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished his purpose, there remains nothing further to be done; if there were anything left to be done, he would not be a knower of reality.
You are not a caste such as a Brahmin, nor do you belong to any stage of life; you are not an object of the senses.
You are unattached, formless, and the witness of the universe—be happy! (56)
When the identification with the body has dissolved and the conscious Self is known,
wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption.
For one who is established in the singular state of the Self, whatever movement there is is its worship;
whatever speech there is is its mantra; and whatever observation there is is its meditation.
Free from conceptualization and discursive thought, with the latent impressions of limiting adjuncts dissolved, that yogi is immersed in his own true nature; he is the knower of the supreme reality.
It causes the body and all the sense organs to function by its mere existence,
just as a magnet acts upon iron within a lamp.

Likewise, the two bodies, as well as the names, castes, and stages of life, are rendered meaningless; through samādhi, [one realizes]: "I am the Brahman that is the earth and the sky—this impurity is [but a delusion]."
How can there be meditation on that which is unmanifest? How can there be the dismissal of that which is all-pervading?
How can there be worship of that which is formless? It is itself the eternal Brahman.
The flower is the cause of the fruit; when the fruit appears, the flower perishes.
Action is the cause of knowledge; when knowledge arises, action perishes.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I take up? What shall I abandon?
Everything is filled by the Self, just as [the world] is filled by the waters of the great dissolution.
One should view the world as having the form of the manifestation of the elements and so forth, both the immobile and the mobile; it is like a magical illusion (indrajāla) and like waves upon water.
Having divided the two parts of the word, one might think it is useless for that which is connected to the object of knowledge;
yet, while it is sometimes possible to speak of the object of knowledge, it is impossible to speak of the [word] as being useless.
He does not harbor pride; he does not disparage others; he does not speak harshly; when something unpleasant is said by anyone, he laughs; and he does not give way to anger.
Upon hearing a poorly composed poem written by another, he remains silent like a mute.
One does not personally take up faults nor commit them; this is the characteristic of the virtuous. // 67 //
Just as a tree exists within the seed and the state of being a seed exists within the tree, so that which is the self of all—the pervaded and the pervader—is not seen as separate [from them]. (68)
The self is one within all beings; how then can bondage and liberation be twofold?
Through the connection with birth and ritual refinement, a state of differentiation exists eternally.
Just as a reflection conforms to its limiting adjunct—whether it be long, horizontal, or circular—the individual soul (jīva) is of a different nature from that; how then could it be one? // 70 //

Just as their birth is determined by their conduct and previous karma, so too, according to their respective capacity for knowledge, there are two types [of beings] regarding bondage and liberation. (71)
Just as this impurity has begun its arising in various forms, so too how could there be oneness regarding pleasures and pains? (72)
A wise person should not consume wealth, nor should he nourish his own possessions;
always content at all times, that man shall become possessed of knowledge. (73)
The body is entirely perishable, but the connection is eternal; it moves through various stations by way of the thread of age, just as [a spider] does. (74)
Just as staying in another's house always makes one a mere traveler on the road, even so, a man of knowledge is not touched by pleasure or pain. // 75 //
The actress, the dancing, the drama, the various plays, and the delight—the wise man always knows these to be born of the notion of "I. (76)
Thus ends the determination of knowledge.
Then the listener said:
"What is this that is seen? By whom was it made, and how did it come into being?"
He said to him:
"First, there is the beginningless reality, the conscious Self.
Its manifestation arose, and it then divided this very Self into two."
"In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka [Upaniṣad] it says, 'The husband and the wife became a pair';
and in the [Gāyatrī mantra] which consists of three feet, 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi), that is:
'Thou art That'."
"I am Brahman"—this is the exhalation that extends to the end of the entire universe.
Now, you alone are all of that;
this is a marvel.
Then, make the mind one-pointed and exceedingly subtle;
this is what is called the ultimate truth.
This self is the teacher because it pervades the immovable dharma. Now—
The blind man is lame, and action is established through association;
where there is independence for the lame man, there the blind man becomes fruitless. // 1 //
It is beyond blindness, it is lame yet immovable, and it is eternal;
it is the being that exists both within and without, appearing like space. //2//
However, because they are blinded by *māyā* due to a lack of discrimination,
the two— *jīva* and *Īśvara*— having become one, have falsely created the *brahmāṇḍas* through artifice as well.
Therefore, by abandoning illusion (*māyā*), one abides spontaneously within the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
The authority for this is the Śruti:
"The Self is space; the Void is Brahman."
Now follows the definition of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
Regarding this, the authority is the Śruti:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."
"One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
Now,
it is understood that the consciousness conditioned by the effects [of karma], which is denoted by the term *jīva*, [is the one who eats].
Consciousness conditioned by the causal adjunct is denoted by the term "Īśvara" (the Lord).
This [consciousness] conditioned by the effect-adjunct is the "jīva" (individual soul), while that conditioned by the cause-adjunct is "Īśvara.
Having abandoned the states of being effect and cause, it is established as the full, awakened awareness.
In that context, according to the Vedānta, "effect" refers to the activity of creating the ego and so forth, while "cause" refers to the witness who is the inner radiance. Thus it is said:
"The overseer, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord."
And he is also called the Supreme Self (paramātman), the supreme person (puruṣa) within this body.
Thus [ends the section on] the Lord.
For the Spirit (puruṣa), abiding in Nature (prakṛti), experiences the qualities born of Nature;
the cause of its births in good and evil wombs is its conjunction with these qualities. (2.23)
Thus is the individual soul (jīva).
The reflection of a face seen in a mirror is not distinct from the face itself; indeed, it has no reality as a separate entity.
The presiding individual soul (adhīśajīva), which is the manifestation of consciousness (cidābhāsaka), is likewise; I am that Self whose nature is eternal perception. // 1 //
"Thus in the *Hastāmalaka*:
'In water, one becomes the non-dual beloved.
Thus in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*."
Likewise, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are conceived according to the analogy of the original object and its reflection.

He states the means for the liberation of that individual soul: one should perform the ritual duties (*karma*), specifically, "one should worship the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) daily until the end of life; one should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice as long as one lives;
one who desires heaven should perform the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice."
"Oṃ" is Brahman;
"Oṃ" is this entire universe;
with "Oṃ," one authorizes the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Thus ends the section on action.
Now follows the supreme knowledge:
"Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality."
The first is distinct from the son, wife, wealth, and so forth created by the variegated power of illusion (*māyā*);
the second is distinct from the gross and subtle bodies;
the third is the resolve for liberation alone.
Just as, according to the analogy of the illusory snake in a rope, when such an error persists, he states the means for its liberation:

therein, the true nature and characteristic of the *jīva* appears through the connection with the vision [of the Self], like the light of the sun; that latent impression (*vāsanā*) is the great knot in the heart—this is the characteristic of the *jīva*.

For the sake of the soul’s desire for liberation, the three aims of life (trivarga) and the previously established karma have been taught; now, Pātañjala and Sāṅkhya are being described in brief. // 1 //
Listen to this procedure for worship consisting of the five elements;
it is the threefold action deemed fit for worship in the Pātañjala [Yogaśāstra]. // 2 //
Through the conceit of the body, there is duality; through the state of Sāṃkhya, there is the realization "I am not," which is unity.
Both "I" and "not-I" constitute the cause for the bondage and liberation of sound.
And thus says the Śruti:
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma"; "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman."

Because one observes that the semblances of prior scriptural authority, reasoning, and experience are superseded by the realization of subsequent semblances of scriptural authority, reasoning, and experience, it is generally seen here that a general rule is weaker and the specific exception is stronger; or rather, the prior is sublated by the subsequent. (4)
Thus, in the Vedānta, [the path] culminates in action;
for there is the Śruti stating, "Liberation comes from knowledge alone," and so forth, as well as:
"Indeed, nothing in this world is found to be as purifying as knowledge."
"Their actions are burnt by the fire of knowledge;
all these are indeed of noble birth, but the man of knowledge is My very Self—this is My opinion.
Thus it is supreme knowledge.
Now follows the yoga of action as declared in the Vedas:

the dharma of the social classes and stages of life, preceded by the injunctions of the Vedas and other scriptures; that [dharma] is either achievable or unachievable, and it bestows the fruits of actions resulting in rebirth. // 1 //

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there may be a "sarga" (emission) intended for the ritual act so that it might be heard; however, being subject to prohibitions and injunctions, [the self] does not become a means for the attainment of liberation. // 2 //
Through the means of recitation (japa) and performance (anuṣṭhāna), there shall be the grace of the deity;
from that [grace], there shall arise accomplishment (siddhi) devoid of the limiting adjunct of consciousness (caitanya-upādhi). // 3 //

Among those, the worship of the elements (*bhūtapūjā*) consists of pilgrimages to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*) such as those of kings and immovable objects, as well as the *agnihotra*, *jvālāmukhī-yāga*, and so forth.
The worship of water (*ap-pūjā*) consists of the veneration of the waters of the Gaṅgā, the Naimiṣa forest, and other such places. And thus it is said:
The *Saṃhitā*, the *Brāhmaṇa*, the *Āraṇyaka*, the *Dvandvadīkṣā*,
the *Nighaṇṭuka*, as well as *Jyotiṣa* and *Nirukta*— these ten works constitute the *Sūtra*.
The entire world is bound by a single knot of the *liṅga*;
when it is bound by ten knots, how can there be liberation for it? (5)
Thus one recites the *haṃkāra* of the Vedas for the nourishment of the body;
having known this supreme knowledge, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. // 6 //
But the *saṃhitā* is the activity, and the *chandas* is the Brahman that is perceived;
having taken refuge in the forest of the sky, one realizes through the statement "I am the *chandas*-Brahman. (7)
The restraint of the mind and so forth, the training, the glossary, the maintenance of conduct, solitude, and the light— this is called my Sūrya.
He who knows the Nirukta, that which cuts through doubt, the recitation of the Sūtras, the wisdom of knowledge, the adjuncts such as food, and the Vedas and so forth— he is a knower of the Veda.
The meaning of this is as follows: *saṃhitā* means one's own welfare;
it transcends cause and effect, and is not an injunction for ritual action.
*Brāhmaṇa* means the totality of Brahman itself, and not sacrifice and so forth.

"Forest-dwelling" (āraṇya) means taking the sky as one's objective, not weeping in the wilderness. "Vedic meter" (chandas) means the remembrance that "I am Brahman," not the deceptive incantations of a goblin. "Training" (śikṣā) means the instruction of mental concentration and so forth, not mere recitation. "Glossary" (nighaṇṭu) means firmness and vigilance in conduct, not wandering to foreign lands.
That which is called *jyotiṣa* consists in discernment, not in the professional activity of astrologers and the like;
that which is called *sūtra* consists in the continuous connection of non-duality, not in the incitement to ritual action;
and that which is called *nirukta* consists in the cutting away of doubt, not in mere proficiency in the meaning of the Vedas.
What is called the recitation of the sūtras is the vision of knowledge, not the power of grammar.
This knowledge is supreme knowledge; any other [knowledge] merely nourishes saṃsāra.
Thus concludes the yoga of action as declared in the Vedas;
its authority rests on the Vedic text: "One attains union, similarity of form, and residence in the same world."
Now follows the Pātañjala Haṭhayoga.
Now he explains the Yoga of Patañjali, its limbs in due order. Liberation is to be accomplished through the body; hear that knowledge which is the means to it. (1)

In that regard, the *Haṃsopaniṣad* states: Having pressed the anus and raised the vital air (*vāyu*) from the *ādhāra*, having circumambulated the *svādhiṣṭhāna* three times to the right, having gone to the *maṇipūraka*, having passed beyond the *anāhata*, and having restrained the breaths in the *viśuddha*, one should meditate upon the *brahmarandhra* following the *ājñā*.

Therein, one experiences the *nāda*: first is *ciṇiti* (1), then *ciṇiciṇi* (2), *ghaṇṭā* (3), *śaṅkha* (4), *tantrī* (5), *tāla* (6), *veṇu* (7), *bherī* (8), *mṛdaṅga* (9), and *megha* (10). One should abandon the ninth and practice the tenth.
Therefore, the mind becomes dissolved.
He whose mind does not perceive the obstruction within the mind that resides in the mind; he whose body is the mind, who controls the mind from within;
[he perceives] the wheel, the seven, the three peaks, as well as the illustrious Haṭha and Go-haṭha.
The knitting of the eyebrows is the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra); the stake is Jālandhara, the vehicle. // 1 //
Ṭālī, lolī, and likewise dhotī; the purification of the uvula (lambikā) in due order; khecarī, bhūcarī, and likewise mahākāṣṭhā. // 2 //
Udgāna, Lopana, Gāṭhana, Avakāśaka, and [the others]—these are the names of the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs], twenty-eight in sequential order. // 3 //
Uttering the *praṇava* while reciting the mantra "so 'haṃ yāmaḥ" according to another tradition,
the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes the agent of this [practice], which is considered the vessel for the body;
through this means, perfection is attained, and one is born as an ancient sage (*vṛddha*).
For them, there shall be the powers beginning with *aṇimā*, as well as the past, future, and present;
the perfection of speech, death, liberation, and honor through association with the body.
Just as patience is the characteristic mark of a deceased person and happiness arises from his presence,
so too, through the vital breath within the body, there arises the conceit of "I" and "mine."
When the vital breath has reached the aperture of Brahmā, liberation indeed arises;
just as the master of a house, fleeing from a burning dwelling, attains happiness. // 7 //
Furthermore, the abiding of egoism is the latent impression that grants birth; likewise, liberation residing within the body is a notion held only by the ignorant. (8)
In this regard, as it is said in the Gītā:
"Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new,"
In the same way, the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new. (9)
When the seer and the seen exist within the body through attachment, how can the embodied self be liberated? How can it be distinct from everything, being all-pervading by nature? 10.

Therefore, the yogi who has blossomed [in realization] is rendered deficient by the Kaula teaching; other [practices], such as the simultaneous arising [of breaths] and so forth, are useless due to attachment to the body. 11.
The Self is consciousness, bliss, eternal, pure, and free from affliction; it should always be understood as transcending the body through mere cognition. 12.
As long as there is identification with the body and as long as spiritual accomplishment continues to proceed, so long will there be the giving of births in accordance with one's karma. // 13 //
In that regard, the scriptural passage expressing the sense of negation is:
"Not by action, not by progeny, nor by wealth,
but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality."
Placed beyond the sky in the secret cave, it shines brilliantly— that which the ascetics enter.
"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified"—so says the Śruti.
"From the world up to the realm of Brahmā"—so it is said in the Gītā.
Or rather, it is that place where there occurs the cessation of all that is desired, unseen, or visible.
Therefore, the Self, being distinct from that [object], is indeed directly manifest by itself. // 1 //
As long as the sage does not know the Self, which is the gain of agency, all [his practices] will be as futile as a barren woman adorned with ornaments. // 2 //
Thus, one who is devoted to ritual action,
however, brings about misfortune and causes the destruction of the body;
therefore, one should practice for the sake of knowledge.
In that context, the "wheel" (cakra) is the body, which is called the support (ādhāra). // 1 //
The self-establishment (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the sattvic ego (ahaṅkāra). // 2 //
Maṇipura is the intellect (buddhi). // 3 //
The Unstruck Sound is right conduct. // 4 //
Pure devotion to Guha. // 5 //
In the wheel of command, there is attentiveness toward gnosis. // 6 //
The thousand-petaled [lotus] is the fourth state.
The three peaks are devoid of qualities. // 8 //
Śrīhaṭha is free from illusion (māyā). // 9 //
The "cow-stall" is the concealment by ignorance. // 10 //
The knitting of the eyebrows is devoid of desire. // 11 //
The aperture of Brahmā is the dissolution of the mind. // 12 //
The "stake-binding" is the restraint of the senses. // 13 //
The vehicle is the relinquishing of sense objects. // 14 //
Jālandhara is devoid of self and other. // 15 //
It is devoid of any discussion regarding the nature of entities. // 16 //
Lolī is the practice of moderate eating. // 17 //
The *dhotī* is unity even in all waters. // 18 //
The lambikā is free from praise and blame. // 19 //
The gaze is fixed on the empty space [of the sky] in the practice of Khecarī. // 20 //
The Bhūcarī [mudrā] consists of a mere glance for a duration of two finger-joints. // 21 //
The Great Quarter is the certainty that "all is Brahman. // 22 //
Singing without a dwelling. // 23 //
Omission is that which has passed beyond its function. // 24 //
Gāṭhana is the endurance of physical suffering. // 25 //
Grant me the space that transcends the body. // 26 //
The names of the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs]. // 27 // 28 //
Devoid of conceptual proliferation and discursive thought.
Thus should the wise person practice, and not merely the physical semblance of a body;
for human beings wander in vain, [failing to realize that] the Self is distinct from the body.
Thus concludes the Patañjala Haṭhayoga.
Now follows the King of Sāṅkhya Yoga:
Without Sāṅkhya, direct realization cannot occur for those yogis of the Self;
the body, like a sheath, must be cast off, so that one's own nature shines forth like the sky. (1)
That which the Śaivas worship as Śiva, the Vedāntins as Brahman, the Buddhists— skilled in the means of valid cognition— as the Buddha, the Naiyāyikas as the Creator,
the followers of the Jaina teaching as the Arhat, and the Mīmāṃsakas as Karma; [that is this very one].
All [schools] are intent on the state of dissolution and devoid of conceptual proliferation; there is nothing other than that which is beyond Sāṃkhya. // 2 //
"One should thoroughly practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga [to realize] the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa)"—this is the Vedic statement (śruti) spoken by the virtuous through the Vedāntas. // 3 //
Sāṃkhya fills the space, while Yoga fills the breath;
the Self is distinct from the body; therefore, one should thoroughly practice Sāṃkhya. // 4 //
The dissolution of all those words [is] the state of being distinct from the Self;
that which is designated as Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and anything else, is considered delusive.
For the Self is indeed distinct from all [phenomena], being both one and manifold in form;
it is Brahman alone, without a second, and beyond that there can be nothing further. // 6 //
Thus ends the Sāṃkhya-yoga. Now, the characteristics of the body (deha):
enjoyment, disease, impurity, death, and migration to other fields of experience.
They continue to follow their *prārabdha* (karma already set in motion) exactly as it is; this is indeed certain. // 1 //
The five subtle elements and the gross elements, the entire manifest world, primordial nature, the qualities, and the activities all exist through the illumination of consciousness. (2)
When the mind arises within the body, that action is designated as "living" (jīva); when the mind arises by means of the body, that action is designated as "body" (deha). // 3 //
And the relationship between the eaten and the eater is joined among beings;
for that purpose, my child, hear from me the five elements in their proper order.
Water, earth, and the object of consumption; wind and fire, which are the consumers; therein, space is the receptacle, and existence is designated as pure consciousness alone.
Hunger, thirst, and excretion are merely bodily functions;
other activities are designated by the term "Vedic rites" and are prescribed as such.
Fortitude, equanimity, and desirelessness toward all that is consumed— these,
along with the five unimpaired elements characterized by their respective marks, are said to constitute the body.
In that regard, I am the internal organ;

the "experiencer" (bhoktṛ) is the state of being a witness (sākṣitva) toward the senses; the "means of experience" (bhogasādhanatā) is the examination of tastes (rasaparīkṣā) belonging to the five elements; and the "object of experience" (bhogya) consists of the qualities of substances such as being stout or thin, just as they exist.

In this regard, the authority is the Śruti: "From them he brought forth the Puruṣa; they said, 'Praise the Puruṣa. 'The Puruṣa is indeed the created wealth (vasu); I shall enter according to my proper place,' [he said]; 'Hunger and thirst shall be yours,' so says the Śruti.
Therein, according to the analogy of the mother and child, it is stated in the Gītā: 'This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field (kṣetra). "
Those who know this call him the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). // 8 //
Thus ends the technical terminology of Sāṃkhya (1).

Since this work was thus promised and its printing was undertaken, there are errors in many places due to necessity; however, for the sake of preserving the meaning of the text, we did not direct our attention toward their removal, and the book appears as if fragmentary.
